results.title: GitHub - luferrer/ConfidenceIntervals: Confidence interval computation for evaluation in machine learning using the bootstrapping approach
results.content: Please see the code in the DCA-PLDA github repository (compute\_performance\_with\_confidence\_intervals method) for an example of how to do joint bootstrapping for speaker verification. Evaluation in machine learning is done by computing some performance metric of choice --one that is relevant to our application-- on a test dataset, assuming that this data is representative of the use-case scenario. The time needed to run bootstrapping for system evaluation is then given by the time it takes to compute the metric on a dataset of the size of the original set plus the time needed to create the indices for each bootstrap set, times the number of bootstrap samples we want to use. Then, the lists of metric values resulting from bootstrapping the test data for every seed can be pooled together to obtain a single confidence interval that takes into account both the variation in seed and the variation in test dataset.

results.title: How much does a bootstrap estimate depend on the random number stream?
results.content: This article examines how the random number seed affects the results of a bootstrap analysis by using an example of a small data set that has N=10 observations. I will run the same bootstrap analysis for 50 different seeds and compare the results of a confidence interval. Because we are going to run the same analysis many times with different random number seeds, I will put the bootstrap steps in a SAS macro. Each analysis uses a different seed, which means that the bootstrap resamples are different between the two runs. If you and your colleague run an identical bootstrap analysis but use different seed values, you are likely to obtain results that are similar to each other. In summary, the result of a bootstrap analysis (and ANY statistical technique that uses randomness) depends on the stream of pseudorandom numbers that are used.

results.title: Confidence intervals for accuracy metrics: pros and cons of the bootstrap method compared to variance estimation - Cross Validated
results.content: # Confidence intervals for accuracy metrics: pros and cons of the bootstrap method compared to variance estimation. E.g. multiple-rate-multiple-case (MRMC) studies tend to make it very hard to bootstrap (some solutions still have a bootstrap component, but it's nightmarishly complicated\*), because everything is in a way correlated with everything (you have both the same raters looking at cases, as well as the same cases being looked). It might be possible to fit such a model with something like PROC NLMIXED in SAS and to get confidence intervals that way (they have a decent automatic procedure for SEs there that uses the delta method) in a large study, but the Bayesian approach deals more naturally with (nearly) empty cells. To get guesstimates for other measures that are not simply an observed fraction of a pre-specified number of test cases (such as F1), you could either start with the variance of the binomially distributed simple fractions and do error propagation, or set up simulations (which would be quite similar to bootstrapping).

results.title: simulation - Bootstrap vs other simulated data methods - Cross Validated
results.content: # Bootstrap vs other simulated data methods. In the mixed effect model, many statisticians would like to simulate or bootstrap data to create empirical confidence regions for fixed effect parameters and random effect parameters. $\begingroup$ I don't understand your question. You mention a model and simulating to estimate but don't mention data? Bootstrap requires resampling from the original data and bootstrap is not the same as Monte Carlo on the empirical distribution. If you have data and you don't want to rely on Gaussian assumptions bootstrapping the data using the Monte Carlo approximation is possible. $\begingroup$ You would do that I think if you had a parametric model but no data and wanted to see what a data set from a mixed model would look like under those assumptions. When you have some data you bootstrap, when you don't you simulate multivariate data. * $\begingroup$ If I make it a question would you upvote and give it an accept? To bootstrap in a mixed effects linear model you would do sampling with replacement in a way that maintains the model structure. Once you have done this you have a bootstrap sample. You fit the model to this bootstrap sample and then repeat the bootstrapping followed by model fitting many times. Any time you have a bootstrap histogram of estimates you can construct bootstrap confidence intervals from this collection of estimates. The simplest is Efron's percentile method which takes the 2.5 percentile and the 97.5 percentile from these ordered bootstrap estimate to be the endpoint of a 95% confidence interval. Now in the absence of data you may want to get an understanding of how the model works. then you can do simulation of the data and look at the results in a way similar to what I described for the bootstrap. Find the answer to your question by asking. How does case-resampling bootstrap work for positive-value estimators? 2") Bootstrap to control for confounding variable - sample size. 7") Bootstrap for random effects logistic regression to get CI for difference in proportions. 1") Bootstrapping or permuting as resampling methods for correlations? Comparison of confidence intervals: bootstrap & exact resampling. #### Hot Network Questions.
